intro: The Torah, the first five books of the Bible, is read aloud in synagogues every week, studied in churches, cited in courtrooms and quoted on monuments. Most people know a few of its lines. Few have read it slowly. This unit slows down. You will read the opening of Genesis with a pen in hand, counting names and repeated phrases, and you will read the laws of Exodus, Leviticus and Deuteronomy beside the laws and treaties of Israel's neighbors.

Two questions run through the unit. First, what is actually on the page: the order of events, the names for God, the shape of a chapter, the words a law uses. Second, how careful readers have explained what is there. Jewish tradition, Christian tradition and academic scholarship each have their own answers, and they often begin from the same observation. You will learn the names of those answers, from midrash to the documentary hypothesis, and what evidence each one uses.

By the end you will be able to read a passage of the Torah closely, using four tools: repetition, keyword, structure and gap. You will be able to describe the two creation accounts, the Eden story and its readers, the flood and Babel, the covenant as a treaty, the Ten Commandments in three numberings, the goring ox in two codes, the Shema, the blessings and curses, and the Thirteen Attributes. And you will be able to say, for any reading, whose reading it is.
bigQuestion: What does close reading of the Torah reveal, and how have Jewish, Christian and academic readers made sense of the same words in different ways?

test.q: Which name for God appears throughout Genesis 1:1–2:3?
test.why: Genesis 1 uses Elohim about thirty-five times; "LORD God" begins at Genesis 2:4.

test.q: In Genesis 2, the woman is made
choices: on the sixth day with the man
test.why: Genesis 2 forms the man, plants the garden, makes the animals and then builds the woman from the man's side.

test.q: Genesis Rabbah reads the names Elohim and YHWH as
test.why: The midrash explains the two names as two sides of one God's character, not two sources.

test.q: Which scholar set out the classic four-source hypothesis in 1878?
test.why: Wellhausen's Prolegomena to the History of Israel gave the documentary hypothesis its classic form.

test.q: What does Genesis 1 lack that Enuma Elish has?
test.why: Genesis 1 shares the waters, division and rest but has no combat; God creates by speech alone.

test.q: Which of these is stated in Genesis 3?
choices: The serpent is the most subtle of the beasts
test.why: Only the serpent's subtlety is in the text; apple and Satan come from later readers, and no forgiveness is stated.

test.q: Christian and Jewish readers differ on Eden mainly over
choices: whether sin and guilt are inherited from Adam
test.why: Augustine's original sin has no counterpart in rabbinic tradition, which stresses two inclinations and personal responsibility.

test.q: Which pair of numbers in the flood story do source critics point to?
choices: Two of each animal and seven pairs of clean animals
test.why: Genesis 6:19–20 and 7:2 give different counts, which critics read as two sources spliced together.

test.q: Genesis 11 explains the name Babel by
choices: a pun on the Hebrew for "confuse"
test.why: Genesis 11:9 links Babel to balal, "to confuse"; "gate of the god" is the Babylonian sense.

test.q: Which part of a Hittite treaty does "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt" resemble?
test.why: Exodus 20:2 names the speaker and recalls past rescue, as a treaty's preamble and prologue do.

test.q: Why do Jews, Catholics and most Protestants number the Ten Commandments differently?
choices: The text does not number them
test.why: Exodus 20 gives no numbers; each tradition divides the ten words in its own way.

test.q: In the goring ox laws, which detail is in Exodus but not in Hammurabi?
choices: The owner of a known gorer is liable
The ox is stoned and its flesh not eaten
A slave's death is paid in silver
test.why: Only Exodus 21:28 orders the ox stoned and uneaten; the other elements appear in both codes.

choices: the stranger who lives among you
test.why: Verse 34 says the stranger shall be as one born among you, "and thou shalt love him as thyself."
The verse sets life and death, blessing and cursing before the people and says "choose life."

test.q: The Thirteen Attributes passage follows which event?
test.why: Exodus 34:6–7 comes after the golden calf of Exodus 32, when Moses receives the second tablets.

write.prompt: Does the Torah want its laws read as a treaty between a king and a people, or as something else? Take a position and support it with Exodus 20:2, Deuteronomy 30:19 and one passage of your choice from Exodus 21, Leviticus 19 or Exodus 34. For each passage, say what the text says and how at least one Jewish, Christian or academic reader has read it.
tips: Name each text you cite by book, chapter and verse, and the translation you read it in.
Attribute every belief to its reader: "Jewish tradition holds," "many Christians read," "most scholars think."
Compare readings; do not judge which one is true.
Use the unit's terms: covenant, suzerain, Decalogue, Holiness Code, Thirteen Attributes.
Use at least one close-reading tool by name: repetition, keyword, structure or gap.
